red_flags: Scheme described as an 'identity-theft/MWBE fraud' combining stolen identity information with false MWBE certification
Concurrent prevailing-wage theft on the same public contracts
Parallel insurance-fraud scheme run alongside the certification fraud
Tax evasion charged alongside the fraud scheme
$800,000 restitution agreed at sentencing, indicating a large multi-year scheme
verification_gap: No process independently verified that the identity information used to establish MWBE ownership/eligibility for Eastern Building & Restoration actually belonged to, and was controlled by, the person claimed as the certified MWBE principal.

red_flags: OGS engineer-in-charge approved fraudulent reimbursements on contracts he was responsible for overseeing
Official received over $50,000 in construction equipment and home-improvement materials as payment
Fictitious/inflated invoices submitted across 16 separate state-prison emergency-repair contracts
Labor-hour inflation used to pad billed amounts
verification_gap: No independent, arms-length reviewer outside the approving engineer-in-charge verified labor hours and invoiced amounts against actual work performed on the emergency-repair contracts before reimbursement was authorized.

red_flags: False reimbursement claims submitted with altered invoices
Claimed rental fees for equipment the company already owned
Pattern repeated across 10 contracts over three years
Emergency-work designation used for the fraudulent claims
verification_gap: No verification matched claimed equipment-rental invoices against the contractor's own equipment-ownership records before reimbursing the rental fees.

red_flags: Fraudulent certified payroll statements submitted to NYPA
Billed for employees who performed no work
Scheme ran under a five-year, $3M landscaping/maintenance contract
Filed a tax return substantially understating income from the scheme
verification_gap: NYPA did not cross-check certified payroll submissions against independent proof of employee presence (e.g., site logs or time records) to confirm the listed workers actually performed the billed hours.

red_flags: NYPA insider overseeing the contract helped the contractor bill for non-existent employees
Insider personally diverted worker wages and concealed his own cut
False tax filings used to hide the concealed proceeds
Scheme required coordination among three co-defendants and Over Rock Construction
verification_gap: NYPA had no independent check ensuring the contract-overseeing insider was not personally profiting from the certified-payroll submissions he was responsible for reviewing and approving.

red_flags: Maintenance supervisor personally selected contractors and gathered bids for OMH work
Accepted bribes from a contractor to rig bids on seven projects
Sister with administrative access allegedly assisted the scheme
Scheme spanned multiple projects (2004-2006) at Manhattan Psychiatric Center
verification_gap: No segregation of duties separated the employee who solicited and gathered competing bids from the decision on which contractor was ultimately awarded the work, letting one person control both sides of the bid process.

red_flags: DEC project manager used his oversight authority to solicit money for electrical work
Diverted solicited funds through shell companies he personally controlled
Separately orchestrated a fraudulent bank loan through a contractor
Multiple forgery and grand larceny counts alongside the solicitation conduct
verification_gap: DEC had no independent check on whether its own oversight official held an undisclosed financial interest in companies receiving project-related payments he personally solicited.

red_flags: Falsely certified a minority-owned firm performed $43,807 of plumbing/electrical work
Non-MWBE companies actually performed the work
MWBE firm paid a fee solely to pass through the paperwork
False instrument filing used to document the fictitious MWBE participation
verification_gap: DASNY did not verify, through site records or direct confirmation of who performed the plumbing/electrical work, that the certified MWBE firm actually supplied the labor it was credited with.

red_flags: IG found MWBE documentation may have been altered
Subcontractor's role was mischaracterized to inflate MWBE credit
Prime contractor claimed MWBE credit it wasn't entitled to
IG recommended DASNY adjust the MWBE utilization credits
verification_gap: DASNY did not independently verify the submitted MWBE documentation and the subcontractor's actual scope of work against the credit claimed before applying it toward MWBE utilization goals.

red_flags: DMYLES (MBE subcontractor) was never actually involved in furnishing/installing the granite seat-wall
Totaro Inc. performed all the real work
DMYLES collected a 5% pass-through fee for no commercially useful function
Scott Lawn Yard claimed MWBE credit it hadn't earned
verification_gap: DASNY had no mechanism confirming DMYLES performed a commercially useful function on site, rather than merely invoicing a fee, before crediting the prime contractor with MWBE participation.

red_flags: Same pass-through pattern as the Scott Lawn Yard case, published the same day
DMYLES again functioned as a pass-through MBE subcontractor
Prestige Countertops actually performed the bathroom-rehab work
Javen Construction claimed MWBE credit for work the credited firm did not do
verification_gap: DASNY lacked a repeatable check to confirm that a subcontractor already implicated in a prior pass-through finding (DMYLES) was performing real, commercially useful work rather than passing through invoices on a second project.

red_flags: Invoices submitted to DASNY had been doctored to inflate billed amounts
Inflation totaled $33,000 across three separate billing cycles
Scheme ran over several months (Oct 2022-Jan 2023) before detection
verification_gap: DASNY's invoice-review process caught the doctored invoices before full reimbursement, but no upfront verification of underlying billing documentation existed to prevent doctored invoices from being submitted across three cycles in the first place.

red_flags: Concealed that required bridge-sealing chemicals were never purchased
Billed NYSDOT for $1.9M+ in contract work despite the non-performance
Scheme ran across federally funded contracts since 2010
Wire and mail fraud charges reflect the fraudulent billing
verification_gap: NYSDOT did not verify contractor purchase/delivery records for the required bridge-sealing chemicals against amounts billed before paying for the sealing work.

red_flags: Case centers on the SUNY Polytechnic/Fort Schuyler 'Buffalo Billion' procurement scheme
Wire fraud conspiracy charges against developer executives and the SUNY Poly official
Original convictions vacated and required new, narrower plea agreements nine years later
Large forfeiture ($1.6M) tied to the procurement-related conduct
verification_gap: The Fort Schuyler/SUNY Poly RFP process had no independent check preventing an insider from shaping request-for-proposal criteria to favor pre-selected developers before bids were solicited.

red_flags: Bribes disguised as his wife's low-show job at an energy company
Payments funneled through COR Development, a developer with pending state business before him
Used influence over state economic-development decisions in exchange for payments
Expedited delayed state funding to COR in exchange for the bribes
verification_gap: The Executive Chamber had no disclosure/verification process to catch a senior aide's household receiving undisclosed compensation (a spouse's job) from entities with pending state economic-development decisions before him.

red_flags: Falsified subcontractor change orders submitted as billing support
Inflated payment requests submitted across at least four public projects
Scheme ran roughly five years (Dec 2017-Dec 2022) before resolution
Resolved via $1.5M forfeiture deferred-prosecution agreement rather than a straight prosecution
verification_gap: CUNY/York College did not independently verify submitted subcontractor change orders against actual subcontractor work and agreements before approving the inflated payment requests.

red_flags: Program manager secretly operated a shell consulting company registered in his children's names
Company operated while he ran the same Superstorm Sandy contracts it stood to benefit from
Deleted evidence and coached witnesses to lie once investigated
A later OIG report found the same shell company received a no-bid subcontract from a vendor with undisclosed ties to in-house consultants
verification_gap: MTA had no beneficial-ownership disclosure check on vendors/consultants that would have flagged the program manager's undisclosed financial interest in a company tied to contracts he personally ran.

red_flags: 34-year construction manager steered contract oversight to benefit family members
Nephew with no construction experience placed as safety supervisor on a $14.6M renovation
Brother employed by the contractor on a separate $3.9M roof-repair contract
Neither family relationship was disclosed
verification_gap: MTA had no conflict-of-interest disclosure check cross-referencing contract-oversight staff's family members against personnel placed on, or employed by vendors on, the same contracts.

red_flags: Five employees claimed hundreds of overtime hours never actually worked
One employee was bowling while purportedly on duty
Another was on vacation during claimed overtime hours
Scheme was detected only via cell-location data, badge-swipe records, and third-party evidence
verification_gap: MTA had no routine cross-check of claimed overtime hours against independent attendance data (badge swipes, location records) at the time hours were submitted, relying instead on after-the-fact investigation to catch the fabricated hours.

red_flags: Falsely reported DBE participation on the Fulton St. Transit Center project
Paid the DBE firm commissions rather than assigning it real subcontract work
Second-tier DBE (J&R Rey) functioned as a pass-through rather than a working subcontractor
verification_gap: MTA/DOT did not verify that the reported DBE subcontractor (J&R Rey) was performing a commercially useful function on-site rather than simply receiving a commission for the use of its certification.

red_flags: Non-DBE subcontractor's (Spectrum) employees were misrepresented as certified DBE (Tower) employees
Scheme ran across two separate MTA/DOT-funded steel-painting jobs
Certified DBE credit was claimed for work performed by a non-certified firm's workforce
verification_gap: MTA/DOT had no process to verify that workers reported under the certified DBE's payroll on the steel-painting jobs were actually employed and directed by that DBE firm rather than by the uncertified subcontractor.

red_flags: Tower Maintenance Corp. (the certified DBE) settled for falsely certifying it performed disguised work
Part of the same three-party Ahern/Spectrum/Tower scheme
Same MTA/DOT steel-painting projects as the Ahern case
verification_gap: MTA/DOT relied on the certified DBE's own self-certification of performance without independently confirming Tower actually supplied the labor it certified on the steel-painting jobs.

red_flags: Spectrum (the non-DBE firm) actually performed the disguised painting work
Settled its own liability in the same three-party DBE scheme as Ahern and Tower
Same MTA/DOT-funded projects as the related Ahern and Tower settlements
verification_gap: MTA/DOT had no check confirming which firm's employees physically performed the steel-painting work, allowing the non-DBE performer's labor to be credited to the certified DBE instead.

red_flags: Roughly $22M in work funneled through a DBE front company
Front company did no actual work on the Maspeth bus depot project
False DBE compliance reported to MTA over a four-year period (2004-2008)
Resulted in over $8 million in forfeiture and penalties
verification_gap: MTA did not verify that the DBE-credited entity was performing real, commercially useful work on the Maspeth bus depot project rather than simply lending its certification to a compliance report.

red_flags: Solicited bribes from two contractors in exchange for steering subway construction work
Threatened to bar contractors from future work if bribe payments stopped
Concealed bribe proceeds via shell accounts
Scheme ran for six years (2009-2015) before detection
verification_gap: MTA/NYCTA had no independent oversight verifying that the Construction Project Administrator's work-steering decisions were free of personal financial inducements from the contractors he oversaw.

red_flags: Contract manager leaked confidential pricing information to a vendor
More than $10M in contracts steered to a single vendor (WRS)
Contract manager received over $70,000 in kickbacks
Vendor's owner required to sell the company as part of his plea
A third individual (Willis) also received probation, indicating a multi-party scheme
verification_gap: Metro-North had no firewall separating staff with access to confidential bid/pricing data from those able to influence vendor selection, so pairing that access restriction with periodic review of contract-award concentration by vendor would have caught the steering before $10M was committed.

red_flags: Certified payrolls showed full prevailing wages while workers were required to kick back roughly 22% in cash
13 workers were required to participate in the kickback scheme
Workers were threatened with reduced hours or termination for refusing to kick back wages
Scheme ran for over four years (Sept. 2020-Dec. 2024) across 9 MTA contracts
verification_gap: The MTA never cross-checked certified payroll filings against independent evidence of what workers actually received, such as confidential wage interviews or bank-deposit verification, so the gap between the paper-perfect certified payrolls and the real cash-kickback arrangement went undetected for over four years.

red_flags: Prevailing-wage fraud paired with bribery, money laundering, and illegal structuring
A union shop steward separately pleaded guilty to taking bribes to look the other way
Contractor ordered to forfeit $7.1M, indicating the scale of concealed proceeds
$1.3M in restitution ordered to the IRS points to underlying tax fraud alongside the wage fraud
verification_gap: SCA and the union relied on the shop steward as the front-line check on certified payroll compliance with no independent, bribe-resistant audit behind him, so once he was paid to look away, falsified certified payrolls passed unchallenged for years.

red_flags: Certified prevailing-wage compliance filed while workers were being underpaid
Scheme spanned four years (2014-2018) on SCA school projects
Restitution, forfeiture, and a separate payment to SCA were ordered, indicating documented underpayment records existed
verification_gap: SCA had no way to independently verify certified payroll submissions against actual wages paid, such as surprise worker interviews or matching payroll records to bank deposits, letting falsified certifications stand unchallenged for four years.

red_flags: Payroll records allegedly used fake names and omitted real workers
Wages inflated on paper while undocumented workers were allegedly paid cash below scale
One defendant allegedly told employees to destroy evidence
Scheme allegedly touched over $13.5M in public-school repair contracts
verification_gap: DOE had no process to verify that names listed on certified payrolls corresponded to real, identifiable workers on site, such as ID checks matched against payroll rosters during site visits, so a roster padded with fictitious names and missing real workers went unchecked.

red_flags: Wage kickback scheme spanned both SCA and NYCHA projects
General contractor Dean Builders paid over $200,000 in restitution for wage underpayment
Singh brothers received a 5-year public-contract ban, indicating deliberate wage theft rather than a bookkeeping error
verification_gap: Neither SCA nor NYCHA cross-verified certified payroll filings from labor brokers against direct worker pay records, letting wage kickbacks on public housing and school sites go undetected until a separate investigation surfaced them.

red_flags: Superintendent convicted of bribery and extortion tied to repair-contract approvals
Bribes collected worth about 10% of each repair contract's value, a consistent kickback rate
One of 70 NYCHA superintendents charged in the same February 2024 sweep, indicating a systemic pattern
Scheme spanned 4 NYCHA developments over 2015-2021
verification_gap: NYCHA had no requirement that repair-contract approvals be countersigned or randomly audited by someone other than the single superintendent who both authorized the work and selected the vendor, letting one person extract a fixed bribe percentage undetected for years.

red_flags: 70 separate NYCHA employees convicted in the same bribery/extortion sweep
Roughly $15M in NYCHA repair contracts affected across the citywide scheme
$2.1M in restitution and $2M in forfeiture ordered, indicating extensively documented bribe proceeds
56 felony pleas, 11 misdemeanor pleas, and 3 trial convictions show the scheme was decentralized across many individual actors
verification_gap: NYCHA lacked a centralized, independently monitored authorization process for repair-contractor selection at the development level, letting dozens of superintendents each independently extract bribes on small repair-contract awards with no cross-development detection mechanism.

red_flags: DEP manager leaked confidential city procurement information to engineering firms
Payments took the form of gifts and subcontracts rather than direct cash
D&B's roughly $1.8M in subcontracts were routed to entities the DEP official secretly controlled
Resolved via a deferred prosecution agreement with an integrity monitor imposed on D&B
verification_gap: DEP had no requirement for procurement staff to disclose financial interests in subcontracting entities receiving city-funded work, so a manager could route subcontracts to companies he secretly controlled without any conflict-of-interest disclosure check flagging the connection.

red_flags: Original charges were pay-to-play bribery/corruption, 5 counts
Case was tied to the same D&B/DEP procurement-leak scheme
Conviction was ultimately vacated and dismissed, citing mishandled evidence and pandemic-era court constraints
verification_gap: The case record shows a downstream evidentiary failure rather than a missing agency control: even where an investigation identified alleged pay-to-play payments, the prosecution's evidence-handling process failed to preserve proof strong enough to sustain the bribery conviction, so no verification step within DEP itself is confirmed by this outcome either way.

red_flags: Falsely certified that a licensed Master Electrician supervised code-required work
Unlicensed personnel actually performed the supervised work
Over $200M in NYC water-infrastructure contracts secured under the false certification
False instrument filing charge confirms fabricated certification documents were submitted
verification_gap: DEP never independently verified that the specific licensed Master Electrician named in supervision filings was actually present on site performing or overseeing the code-required work, letting a paper certification substitute for real licensed supervision across two major capital projects.

red_flags: Program manager took roughly $500,000 in bribes from a subcontractor over five years
Bribes were exchanged for allowing overbilling on repair work
Signed off on incomplete or unperformed repairs
Managed a Water Board program covering sewer/water lateral repairs for homeowners
verification_gap: The NYC Water Board had no independent field verification, such as homeowner sign-off or third-party inspection, confirming that lateral repairs billed as complete had actually been performed before Djurasevic's sign-off was accepted as sufficient proof of completion.

red_flags: Two DOT officials leaked the City's confidential negotiating position to a contractor
Bribes of $60,000 and $5,000 were paid to the two officials
Leaked information was used to steer a roughly $16.5M contract-claim settlement favorably to the contractor
verification_gap: DOT had no segregation between the officials who held the City's confidential settlement negotiating position and those permitted to interact with the contractor's negotiators, so bribed officials could hand that position to the other side undetected.

red_flags: Decade-long (1999-2009) scheme of padding client bills with unworked 'guaranteed' overtime
Billed for absent employees
Charged above-contract rates
Paid over $20.2 million combined in restitution and penalties
verification_gap: The Port Authority never reconciled Tishman's billed labor hours, including the 'guaranteed' overtime, against independent timekeeping or site-attendance records, allowing a decade of padded and absent-employee billing to go unchallenged.

red_flags: 136 felony counts stemmed from submitted certified payroll records
Falsely claimed $268,056 in union benefits had been paid to workers
Benefits certified as paid were never actually disbursed to the union funds
verification_gap: The Port Authority had no process to verify directly with the union benefit funds that the contributions certified as paid on Padover's payroll filings had actually been received, letting falsely certified benefit payments go unverified across 136 counts.

red_flags: Falsely represented that certified minority/women-owned subcontractors performed steel-decking and surveying work
DCM Erectors actually performed the work itself
Paid front-entity principals to look the other way
Conviction later vacated, with the court finding no proof the M/WBE misrepresentation caused economic harm
verification_gap: The Port Authority's M/WBE compliance monitoring had no on-site verification that the certified minority/women-owned firms listed on the contract were the ones actually performing the steel-decking and surveying work, allowing DCM to self-perform while paying the front entities to sign off.

red_flags: Secretly controlled Crimson Construction while concealing that control from the Port Authority
Concealed ties to the Bonanno organized-crime family
Diverted over $1.5 million of contract proceeds for personal use
Crimson ultimately failed its contract obligations and was terminated
verification_gap: The Port Authority's contractor-integrity vetting had no mechanism to verify the true beneficial ownership and control of Crimson Construction beyond its nominal officers, so Vertuccio's concealed control and organized-crime ties went undetected until the company defaulted.

red_flags: Board Chairman had a proposed capital-construction agreement pulled from the board agenda
Agenda item restored only after United reinstated a money-losing nonstop route for his personal convenience
United separately paid a $2.25 million penalty tied to the same conduct
verification_gap: The Port Authority board had no process requiring the chairman to recuse from or disclose personal interest in agenda decisions involving a vendor providing him a direct personal benefit, letting one chairman unilaterally control the timing of a tenant's capital-agreement approval.

red_flags: Manager accepted roughly $17,000 in tickets, golf trips, and car service
Received confidential bid/budget information and preferential treatment in exchange
Unqualified electricians were hired through personal connections
Unqualified hires created safety hazards while being paid $1.26 million total from Port Authority funds
verification_gap: Cushman & Wakefield and the Port Authority had no gift-disclosure or bid-information access log for the manager overseeing WTC electrical work, so repeated non-cash gifts tied to confidential budget disclosures went unflagged until charged criminally.

red_flags: Systematically inflated invoices on time-and-expense contracts from 2013-2018
Billed more hours than employees actually worked
Scheme surfaced only through a whistleblower qui tam suit, not agency detection
Accepted a five-year debarment from NY public contracts as part of the settlement
verification_gap: The MTA, Port Authority, and SCA had no process reconciling VJA's billed inspector hours against independent time records such as badge or site logs on time-and-expense contracts, letting five years of inflated billing go undetected until an insider filed a qui tam suit.

red_flags: Selection committee members received free home renovations, electronics, and jewelry
Bribes exchanged for votes awarding the renovation contract to a specific contractor
Helped the contractor fraudulently inflate change orders to recoup the cost of the bribes
Contract awarded by a tenant airline within its own leased terminal space, outside direct Port Authority award control
verification_gap: The tenant airline's contractor-selection committee had no conflict-of-interest disclosure or gift-reporting requirement for members voting on contract awards, and change orders were not independently verified against actual scope changes, letting bribe-driven selection and inflated change orders both go unchecked.

red_flags: Employee influenced contract awards including a $19.7M restroom-renovation contract
Received over $1M in payments for steering contracts
Fraudulent invoices were submitted for non-existent dispatcher services
Continuation of the same Newark Airport contractor-bribery scheme as the 2023 pleas
verification_gap: There was no independent verification that services billed for, such as the dispatcher services, were actually rendered before payment, allowing fraudulent invoices for non-existent work to serve as a channel for kickback payments tied to contract-steering.

red_flags: Suspended NJDOT senior engineer solicited a railway company to submit false invoices
Invoices inflated the bridge rehabilitation cost by roughly $700,000
Split $325,000 in resulting bribes with a middleman
Stripped of his state pension and barred from public employment upon sentencing
verification_gap: NJDOT had no independent engineering review comparing invoiced costs on the Eagle Rock Bridge rehabilitation against a neutral engineer's cost estimate, letting a single senior engineer solicit and approve a $700,000 invoice inflation without cross-check.

red_flags: Attorney acted as middleman soliciting $325,000 in bribes tied to the same Eagle Rock scheme
Bribes were funded by a $700,000 inflation of the bridge project's cost
Convicted at trial of conspiracy, bribery, and fraud
verification_gap: NJDOT had no process flagging unusual third-party involvement, such as an outside attorney brokering payments, in grant-funded invoice approvals, allowing a middleman to broker the kickback split from an inflated invoice undetected.

red_flags: Owner paid roughly $48,000 in cash bribes to a NJDOT engineer
Bribes paid specifically to help win a $44 million NJDOT road-work contract
Charged with both bribery and bid-rigging
Pleaded guilty mid-trial to one count
verification_gap: NJDOT had no separation between the engineer receiving personal cash payments from a bidder and the individuals scoring or awarding the Routes 1 & 9 contract, so a bribed engineer could help steer the $44 million award without an independent, bribe-blind evaluation check.

red_flags: Used two shell entities as pass-through disadvantaged business enterprises
Placed magnetic DBE-firm signs on fuel trucks to simulate DBE participation
Falsely claimed DBE credit on a $39 million NJDOT subcontract
Settled for $400,000 with no admission or determination of liability

red_flags: Insurance brokers funneled over $1.5 million in commissions among themselves
Payments made to a firm that 'did no work for the DRPA'
No documentation of services performed to support the commission payments
Broker selection was not competitively bid prior to the report
DRPA spent ~$440 million on economic development despite a charter mandate to prioritize bridge/capital maintenance

red_flags: No dedicated CFO overseeing SCC finances
Only one accountant reviewing nearly all operating expenses
$67 million in 'questionable' land payments to local governments
$328.8 million spent on land acquisition with weak financial review
verification_gap: SCC lacked a segregation-of-duties structure (a dedicated CFO plus independent second-level review) that would have required questionable land payments to be substantiated and approved before disbursement rather than passing through a single accountant's review.

red_flags: Allegedly altered an SCC prequalification notice
Allegedly altered a state Treasury classification form
Charged with forgery and tampering with public records
Used the altered documents to obtain a Hamilton Township school construction contract

red_flags: Collected payments intended for six subcontractors on nine SCC-funded Edison projects
Withheld nearly $1 million owed to those subcontractors
Falsely certified that subcontractors had been paid
Sentenced with $106,000 restitution and debarment from NJ public works

red_flags: Received $1,486,325 in payments on SCC-funded school projects in three districts
Failed to pay subcontractors for work covered by those payments
Indicted for money laundering and misapplication of entrusted property
No later disposition of the indictment could be located

red_flags: Fired 15 long-tenured SDA employees shortly after taking office
Hired friends and relatives into high-paying roles within nine months
Some hires lacked basic qualifications for their positions
Cost over $2.7 million in new salaries

red_flags: Nine different CEOs over two decades at SDA
Unreliable contractor performance reviews despite documented safety issues
SDA-built schools cost 16-24% more than comparable district-run projects
Seven-years-unresolved HVAC failure at Egg Harbor City Middle School
Fifteen-years-nonfunctional fire suppression system at Newark Science Park High School

red_flags: School founder was also board president approving the contract

Steered the contract to the founder's own company, Modern Boat Works
Project was left unfinished

red_flags: Site supervisor submitted inflated overtime timesheets
Business administrator approved the inflated timesheets
Approvals made in exchange for roughly $70,000 in cash kickbacks
Scheme ran on a multimillion-dollar 2019-referendum facilities-upgrade project

red_flags: Alleged use of threats and political pressure to seize control of redevelopment properties

Original charges included racketeering, theft by extortion, and official misconduct
Indictment was dismissed by a Superior Court judge and the appeal and case were later dropped

red_flags: Backdated documents to falsely claim a required joint investment

Exceeded the program's per-investor investment cap
Agreed to pay $5 million penalty and forfeit $1 million in tax credits
Entered a three-year deferred prosecution agreement requiring independent review of future applications

red_flags: Accepted $25,000 in bribes weeks after taking office
Payment came from a cooperating witness posing as a developer
Bribe was exchanged for promised assistance on future redevelopment projects
Part of the federal 'Operation Bid Rig III' sting

red_flags: Accepted $30,000 from an FBI cooperating witness posing as a developer
Payment made in exchange for future assistance on the developer's projects
Pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit extortion
Another conviction from the July 2009 Operation Bid Rig III sting
verification_gap: No independent disclosure or review process existed to catch a council president privately agreeing to help a developer's projects in exchange for cash before any project ever came to a public vote.

red_flags: Accepted $20,000 in illicit campaign contributions from a cooperating witness
Contributions exchanged for using her official position to help a redevelopment project
Convicted by a federal jury (only Bid Rig III defendant to go to trial)

red_flags: Extorted $110,000 from two developers of an affordable housing project
Told developers payments were needed 'to ensure the project would proceed'
Demanded payments even after city approvals were already granted
Sentenced to 27 months and ordered to pay $110,000 restitution; resigned as mayor

red_flags: Directed officials to price a city-owned lot well below its proposed value
Sale was arranged to benefit a cooperating witness's parking garage development
Cash bribes exchanged for the below-market deal
Convicted of extortion, bribery, and mail/wire fraud; sentenced to 58 months

red_flags: Nine-year scheme directing contractors to submit fraudulently inflated and rigged quotes
Scheme spanned school construction/repair projects in three NJ districts
Engineer received over $80,000 in kickbacks for steering the rigged quotes
Co-defendant contractors and a school business administrator also charged with related bribes
verification_gap: Districts relied on the engineer himself to solicit and compare contractor quotes with no independent cross-check of quote patterns across projects, letting the same engineer orchestrate collusive pricing among the same pool of contractors for nine years.

red_flags: Accepted cash and luxury jewelry bribes from two businessmen
Bribes exchanged for help obtaining city-approved redevelopment agreements
Used position as Deputy Mayor/Director of Economic and Housing Development to facilitate acquisition of city-owned properties
Sentenced to 12 months and one day in prison
verification_gap: There was no independent, disclosed-gifts review for the city official negotiating redevelopment agreements, allowing cash and jewelry to be exchanged privately for help acquiring city-owned properties without triggering any conflict check.

red_flags: Paid 27 workers $15-$25/hour against a required Davis-Bacon prevailing wage of $61.50-$82.31

Payments made to limit SCA scrutiny of the project

red_flags: Misclassified five employees into lower-paying job categories on certified payrolls

red_flags: Falsified certified payroll documents on multiple Long Island public school-construction contracts

red_flags: Two officers accepted about $40,000 combined for approving contractor payment requests

red_flags: Paid workers $120-$160/day for 40-50 hour weeks, far below prevailing wage

red_flags: Certified payroll reports claimed $54/hour plus $40.16-$51.86 in benefits paid to workers

red_flags: Failed to pay required prevailing wage and supplemental-benefit rates to over 200 workers

red_flags: Underpaid workers below the legally required prevailing wage on multiple concurrent public-works contracts

red_flags: Altered workers'-compensation exemption forms to falsely claim the company had no employees requiring coverage

red_flags: Chaired the committee that selected Hill International without disclosing a longstanding close personal friendship with Hill VP Thomas Foy
